said: By twenty thirty, data centers could use about as much electricity as all of Japan uses today, according to the International Energy Agency. Imagine you're building a new city.
She's helping wire one of the biggest computer buildings ever made. Rows and rows of machines, packed with the chips that power artificial intelligence.
The biggest tech companies, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, are spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on data centers and chips.
Their leaders have said it plainly. The risk of spending too little is bigger than the risk of spending too much.
The company selling most of those chips is NVIDIA. In twenty twenty-five, it became the first company in history worth five trillion dollars.
Its top AI chips can cost tens of thousands of dollars each. A single large data center can hold hundreds of thousands of them.
And the buildings need power. So much that some tech companies are signing deals to restart old nuclear plants and build new power stations.
In twenty twenty-four, one investor at a big venture firm called this AI's six hundred billion dollar question. That was roughly how much yearly revenue he thought AI needed to justify the spending.
To be fair, AI revenue is growing fast too. OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, has said its yearly revenue reached many billions of dollars. But its spending commitments are far bigger.
Businesses are trying AI everywhere. But a twenty twenty-five study from M I T researchers found that most company AI pilot projects weren't yet showing a clear return.
That's the weak spot. Not whether AI works. Whether enough people and businesses will pay enough for it, fast enough, to cover the bill already being spent.
In the late nineteen nineties, everyone was sure the internet would change the world. They were right.
But they built far more than customers needed. Years later, most of that fiber was still dark, meaning nobody was using it.
When the bubble burst, the Nasdaq stock index fell almost eighty percent. Cisco's stock dropped by more than eighty percent too. Many telecom companies went bankrupt.
And it happened even earlier, with railways in Britain in the eighteen forties. Great technology. Too much building. A painful crash.
The big difference is who's spending. In the dot-com bubble, many companies had no profits at all. Today's biggest AI spenders are some of the most profitable companies ever.
Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta earn huge amounts from software, ads and cloud services. Much of their AI spending comes from profits they already have.
For example, in twenty twenty-five, NVIDIA said it would invest up to one hundred billion dollars in OpenAI. OpenAI, in turn, plans to buy huge amounts of NVIDIA chips.
Some data centers are also being paid for with big loans and bonds. Debt is fine when revenue arrives on time. It's dangerous when it doesn't.
Then stock prices would fall. And because a handful of tech giants now make up a huge share of the whole stock market, almost every index fund would feel it.
